turns.response_html:
While it is rare to see centipedes moving in a "group" (as they are generally solitary and cannibalistic), house centipedes are among the fastest arthropods for their size.

Speed and Velocity

A house centipede (Scutigera coleoptrata) can travel at speeds of up to 1.3 feet per second (roughly 0.4 meters per second).

  • To put that in perspective, if a house centipede were the size of a human, it would be sprinting at over 40 mph.
  • This speed is achieved through their 15 pairs of long, specialized legs that prevent them from tripping over themselves.

The "Layering" Movement Technique

The "layering" or "metachronal" movement technique refers to the way centipedes coordinate their legs in waves to maintain high speeds without losing balance.

  • Metachronal Waves: Centipedes move their legs in a sequence where each leg is slightly out of phase with the one behind it. This creates a ripple effect that looks like a wave traveling down the body.
  • Body Undulation: House centipedes are unique because they have shortened back plates (tergites) that overlap. This rigid structure prevents their bodies from "snaking" or swaying side-to-side at high speeds, allowing all energy to go into forward momentum.
  • Leg Length Variation: Their legs actually get longer toward the rear of the body. This prevents the back legs from stepping on the front legs, effectively "layering" their stride patterns so they can maintain a high-speed gallop without tangling.

Because of this sophisticated mechanical coordination, house centipedes can stop and change direction almost instantly, making them incredibly effective hunters.

It sounds like you might be describing "collective locomotion" or "non-cooperative swarming." While centipedes are solitary hunters, certain species of millipedes and some larvae (like fungus gnat larvae) are known for this fascinating "stacking" behavior.

The Mechanics of the "Moving Carpet"

When these creatures stack and crawl over one another, the group can actually move faster than any individual could on its own. It is a bit like a pedestrian walkway at an airport:

  • The Velocity Add-on: If an insect on the ground moves at a speed of $v$, and another insect crawls on top of it at that same speed $v$, the one on top is effectively moving at $2v$ relative to the ground.
  • The "Tread" Effect: As the ones at the back crawl to the front and the ones at the bottom are left behind, the entire "blob" or "carpet" progresses forward.
  • Efficiency: This layering helps the group navigate over obstacles that would be too tall for a single individual to climb, and it offers protection by making the group look like one large, intimidating organism rather than thousands of tiny ones.

turns.prompt_text: how do I keep them out of my living space
turns.response_html:
To keep house centipedes out, focus on removing moisture and sealing entry points. Use a dehumidifier in damp areas like basements and clear away leaf litter or wood piles from your home's exterior.

  • Seal Cracks: Use caulk to close gaps in baseboards, window frames, and doors.
  • Dry It Out: Fix leaky pipes and ensure bathrooms are well-ventilated.
  • Remove Food: Since they eat other bugs, eliminating spiders and silverfish effectively starves them out.

Sticky traps placed along floorboards can also help you monitor where they are entering.
